n: *Translator's note:* *Heb* “And look, he was standing by the Nile, and look, from the Nile were coming up seven cows, attractive of appearance and fat of flesh.” By the use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”), the narrator invites the audience to see the dream through Pharaoh’s eyes.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And look, seven other cows were coming up after them from the Nile, bad of appearance and thin of flesh.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Nile.” This has been replaced by “the river” in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And look, a dream.”

*Study note:* Pharaoh’s two dreams, as explained in the following verses, pertained to the economy of Egypt. Because of the Nile River, the land of Egypt weathered all kinds of famines—there was usually grain in Egypt, and if there was grain and water the livestock would flourish. These two dreams, however, indicated that poverty would overtake plenty and that the blessing of the herd and the field would cease.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his spirit.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he sent and called,” which indicates an official summons.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term חַרְטֹם (khartom) is an Egyptian loanword (hyr-tp) that describes a class of priests who were skilled in such interpretations.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has the singular (though Smr reads the plural). If retained, the singular must be collective for the set of dreams. Note the plural pronoun “them,” referring to the dreams, in the next clause. However, note that in v. {{Genesis 41:15|15}} Pharaoh uses the singular to refer to the two dreams. In vv. {{Genesis 41:17|17-24}} Pharaoh seems to treat the dreams as two parts of one dream (see especially v. {{Genesis 41:22|22}}).

*Translator's note:* “there was no interpreter.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for Pharaoh.” The pronoun “him” has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “sins, offenses.” He probably refers here to the offenses that landed him in prison (see {{Genesis 40:1|40:1}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he, each according to the interpretation of his dream we dreamed.”

*Translator's note:* Or “slave.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a servant to the captain of the guards.” On this construction see GKC 419-20 §129.*c*.

*Translator's note:* The words “our dreams” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he interpreted for us our dreams, each according to his dream he interpreted.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “interpreted.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Pharaoh) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “him”; the referent (the baker) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Pharaoh sent and called,” indicating a summons to the royal court.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “dreamed a dream.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “there is no one interpreting.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “saying.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you hear a dream to interpret it,” which may mean, “you only have to hear a dream to be able to interpret it.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “not within me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “God will answer.”

*Translator's note:* The expression שְׁלוֹם פַּרְעֹה (shelom parʿoh) is here rendered “the welfare of Pharaoh” because the dream will be about life in his land. Some interpret it to mean an answer of “peace”—one that will calm his heart, or give him the answer that he desires (cf. NIV, NRSV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “In my dream look, I was standing.” The use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”) here (and also in vv. {{Genesis 41:18|18}}, {{Genesis 41:19|19}}, {{Genesis 41:22|22}}, {{Genesis 41:23|23}}) invites the hearer (within the context of the narrative, Joseph, but in the broader sense the reader or hearer of the Book of Genesis) to observe the scene through Pharaoh’s eyes.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and look, from the Nile seven cows were coming up, fat of flesh and attractive of appearance, and they grazed in the reeds.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “And look.”

*Translator's note:* The word “cows” is supplied here in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when they went inside them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it was not known.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and I saw in my dream and look.”

*Translator's note:* The words “all this” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and there was no one telling me.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the dream of Pharaoh is one.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “declared.”

*Translator's note:* The active participle here indicates what is imminent.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “are.” Another option is to translate, “There will be seven years of famine.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it is the word that I spoke.”

*Translator's note:* The perfect with the vav consecutive continues the time frame of the preceding participle, which has an imminent future nuance here.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb כָּלָה (kalah) in the Piel stem means “to finish, to destroy, to bring an end to.” The severity of the famine will ruin the land of Egypt.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and concerning the repeating of the dream to Pharaoh two times.” The Niphal infinitive here is the object of the preposition; it is followed by the subjective genitive “of the dream.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “established.”

*Translator's note:* The clause combines a participle and an infinitive construct: God “is hurrying…to do it,” meaning he is going to do it soon.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “let Pharaoh look.” The jussive form expresses Joseph’s advice to Pharaoh.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man discerning and wise.” The order of the terms is rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and let him set him.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verbal form has an obligatory nuance here. Smr has a jussive form here, “and let [Pharaoh] do.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and let him appoint.” The jussive form expresses Joseph’s advice to Pharaoh.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “appointees.” The noun is a cognate accusative of the preceding verb. Since “appoint appointees” would be redundant in English, the term “officials” was used in the translation instead.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he shall collect a fifth of the land of Egypt.” The language is figurative (metonymy); it means what the land produces, i.e., the harvest.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the food.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “under the hand of Pharaoh.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[for] food in the cities.” The noun translated “food” is an adverbial accusative in the sentence.

*Translator's note:* The perfect with vav (ו) consecutive carries the same force as the sequence of jussives before it.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the land will not be cut off in the famine.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the matter was good in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of all his servants.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like this,” but the referent could be misunderstood to be a man like that described by Joseph in v. {{Genesis 41:33|33}}, rather than Joseph himself. For this reason the proper name “Joseph” has been supplied in the translation.

*Translator's note:* The rhetorical question expects the answer “No, of course not!”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “as discerning and wise.” The order has been rearranged in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and at your mouth (i.e., instructions) all my people will kiss.” G. J. Wenham translates this “shall kowtow to your instruction” (*Genesis* [WBC], 2:395). Although there is some textual support for reading “will be judged, ruled by you,” this is probably an attempt to capture the significance of this word. Wenham lists a number of references where individuals have tried to make connections with other words or expressions—such as a root meaning “order themselves” lying behind “kiss,” or an idiomatic idea of “kiss” meaning “seal the mouth,” and so “be silent and submit to.” See K. A. Kitchen, “The Term *Nsq* in {{Genesis 41:40|Genesis 41:40}}, ” *ExpTim* 69 (1957): 30; D. S. Sperling, “{{Genesis 41:40|Genesis 41:40}}: A New Interpretation,” *JANESCU* 10 (1978): 113-19.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “only the throne, I will be greater than you.”

*Translator's note:* The translation assumes that the perfect verbal form is descriptive of a present action. Another option is to understand it as rhetorical, in which case Pharaoh describes a still future action as if it had already occurred in order to emphasize its certainty. In this case one could translate “I have placed” or “I will place.” The verb נָתַן (natan) is translated here as “to place in authority [over].”

*Study note:* Joseph became the grand vizier of *the land of Egypt*. See W. A. Ward, “The Egyptian Office of Joseph,” *JSS* 5 (1960): 144-50; and R. de Vaux, *Ancient Israel*, 129-31.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew word שֵׁשׁ (shesh) is an Egyptian loanword that describes the fine linen robes that Egyptian royalty wore. The clothing signified Joseph’s rank.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Pharaoh) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he caused him to ride in the second chariot which was his.”

*Translator's note:* The verb form appears to be a causative imperative from a verbal root meaning “to kneel.” It is a homonym of the word “bless” (identical in root letters but not related etymologically).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “apart from you.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “no man,” but here “man” is generic, referring to people in general.

*Translator's note:* The idiom “lift up hand or foot” means “take any action” here.

*Study note:* The meaning of Joseph’s Egyptian name, *Zaphenath-Paneah*, is uncertain. Many recent commentators have followed the proposal of G. Steindorff that it means “the god has said, ‘he will live’” (“Der Name Josephs *Saphenat-Pa‘neach*,” *ZÄS* 31 [1889]: 41-42); others have suggested “the god speaks and lives” (see BDB 861 s.v. צָפְנָת פַּעְנֵחַ); “the man he knows” (J. Vergote, *Joseph en Égypte*, 145); or “Joseph [who is called] ʾIp-ʿankh” (K. A. Kitchen, *NBD3* 1262).

*Study note:* The name *Asenath* may mean “she belongs to the goddess Neit” (see *HALOT* 74 s.v. אָֽסְנַת). A novel was written at the beginning of the first century entitled *Joseph and Asenath*, which included a legendary account of the conversion of Asenath to Joseph’s faith in Yahweh. However, all that can be determined from this chapter is that their children received Hebrew names. See also V. Aptowitzer, “Asenath, the Wife of Joseph—a Haggadic Literary-Historical Study,” *HUCA* 1 (1924): 239-306.

*Study note:* *On* (also in v. {{Genesis 41:50|50}}) is another name for the city of Heliopolis.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he passed through.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a son of thirty years.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “when he stood before.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “went out from before.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he passed through all the land of Egypt”; this phrase is interpreted by JPS to mean that Joseph “emerged in charge of the whole land.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Joseph) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the food.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “of the seven years which were in the land of Egypt and placed food in the cities.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and Joseph gathered grain like the sand of the sea, multiplying much.” To emphasize the vast amount of grain he stored up, the Hebrew text modifies the verb “gathered” with an infinitive absolute and an adverb.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “before the year of the famine came.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “gave birth for him.”

*Study note:* The name *Manasseh* (מְנַשֶּׁה, menasheh) describes God’s activity on behalf of Joseph, explaining in general the significance of his change of fortune. The name is a Piel participle, suggesting the meaning “he who brings about forgetfulness.” The Hebrew verb נַשַּׁנִי (nashani) may have been used instead of the normal נִשַּׁנִי (nishani) to provide a closer sound play with the name. The giving of this Hebrew name to his son shows that Joseph retained his heritage and faith; and it shows that a brighter future was in store for him.

*Translator's note:* The word “saying” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”

*Study note:* The name *Ephraim* (אֶפְרַיִם, ʾefrayim), a form of the Hebrew verb פָּרָה (parah), means “to bear fruit.” The theme of fruitfulness is connected with this line of the family from Rachel ({{Genesis 30:2|30:2}}) on down (see {{Genesis 49:22|Gen 49:22}}, {{Deuteronomy 33:13|Deut 33:13-17}}, and Hos 13:15). But there is some difficulty with the name “Ephraim” itself. It appears to be a dual, for which F. Delitzsch simply said it meant “double fruitfulness” (*New Commentary on Genesis*, 2:305). G. J. Spurrell suggested it was a diphthongal pronunciation of a name ending in *-*an or *-*am, often thought to be dual suffixes (*Notes on the text of the book of Genesis*, 334). Many, however, simply connect the name to the territory of Ephraim and interpret it to be “fertile land” (C. Fontinoy, “Les noms de lieux en *-*ayim dans la Bible,” *UF* 3 [1971]: 33-40). The dual would then be an old locative ending. There is no doubt that the name became attached to the land in which the tribe settled, and it is possible that is where the dual ending came from, but in this story it refers to Joseph’s God-given fruitfulness.

*Translator's note:* The word “saying” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* Or “for.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to all Egypt.” The name of the country is used by metonymy for the inhabitants.

*Translator's note:* Or “over the entire land”; *Heb* “over all the face of the earth.” The disjunctive clause is circumstantial-temporal to the next clause.

*Text-critical note:* The MT reads “he opened all that was in [or “among”] them.” The translation follows the reading of the LXX and Syriac versions.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the earth,” which refers here (by metonymy) to the people of the earth. Note that the following verb is plural in form, indicating that the inhabitants of the earth are in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “saw.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Jacob.” Here the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Study note:* *Why are you looking at each other?* The point of Jacob’s question is that his sons should be going to get grain rather than sitting around doing nothing. Jacob, as the patriarch, still makes the decisions for the whole clan.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and buy for us from there.” The word “grain,” the direct object of “buy,” has been supplied for clarity, and the words “from there” have been omitted in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* Following the imperatives, the prefixed verbal form with prefixed *vav* expresses purpose of result.

*Translator's note:* The imperfect tense continues the nuance of the verb before it.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “But Benjamin, the brother of Joseph, Jacob did not send with his brothers.” The disjunctive clause highlights the contrast between Benjamin and the other ten.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew verb אָמַר (ʾamar, “to say”) could also be translated “thought” (i.e., “he said to himself”) here, giving Jacob’s reasoning rather than spoken words.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew noun אָסוֹן (ʾason) is a rare word meaning “accident, harm.” Apart from its use in these passages it occurs in {{Exodus 21:22|Exodus 21:22-23}} of an accident to a pregnant woman. The term is a rather general one, but Jacob was no doubt thinking of his loss of Joseph.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “encounters.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the midst of the coming ones.”

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause either introduces a new episode in the unfolding drama or provides the reader with supplemental information necessary to understanding the story.

*Study note:* *Joseph’s brothers came and bowed down before him*. Here is the beginning of the fulfillment of Joseph’s dreams (see {{Genesis 37|Gen 37}}). But it is not the complete fulfillment, since all his brothers and his parents must come. The point of the dream, of course, was not simply to get the family to bow to Joseph, but that Joseph would be placed in a position of rule and authority to save the family and the world ({{Genesis 41:57|41:57}}).

*Translator's note:* The word “faces” is an adverbial accusative, so the preposition has been supplied in the translation.

*Study note:* *But pretended to be a stranger*. Joseph intends to test his brothers to see if they have changed and have the integrity to be patriarchs of the tribes of Israel. He will do this by putting them in the same situations that they and he were in before. The first test will be to awaken their conscience.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “said.”

*Translator's note:* The verb is denominative, meaning “to buy grain”; the word “food” could simply be the direct object, but may also be an adverbial accusative.

*Study note:* *You are spies*. Joseph wanted to see how his brothers would react if they were accused of spying.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to see the nakedness of the land you have come.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they said to him.” In context this is best understood as an exclamation.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he said, ‘No, for the nakedness of the land you have come to see.’” The order of the introductory clause and the direct discourse has been rearranged in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “twelve [were] your servants, brothers [are] we.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “today.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the one is not.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[By] the life of Pharaoh.”

*Study note:* *As surely as Pharaoh lives*. Joseph uses an oath formula to let the brothers know the certainty of what he said. There is some discussion in the commentaries on swearing by the life of Pharaoh, but since the formulation here reflects the Hebrew practice, it would be hard to connect the ideas exactly to Egyptian practices. Joseph did this to make the point in a way that his Hebrew brothers would understand. See M. R. Lehmann, “Biblical Oaths,” *ZAW* 81 (1969): 74-92.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “send from you one and let him take.” After the imperative, the prefixed verbal form with prefixed vav (ו) indicates purpose.

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause is here circumstantial-temporal.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bound.”

*Translator's note:* The words “to see” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the truth [is] with you.”

*Study note:* The same Hebrew word is used for Joseph’s imprisonment in {{Genesis 40:3|40:3}}, {{Genesis 40:4|4}}, {{Genesis 40:7|7}}. There is some mirroring going on in the narrative. The Hebrew word used here (אָסַף, ʾasaf, “to gather”) is not normally used in a context like this (for placing someone in prison), but it forms a wordplay on the name Joseph (יוֹסֵף, yosef) and keeps the comparison working.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Do this.”

*Translator's note:* After the preceding imperative, the imperative with vav (ו) can, as here, indicate logical sequence.

*Study note:* *For I fear God*. Joseph brings God into the picture to awaken his brothers’ consciences. The godly person cares about the welfare of people, whether they live or die. So he will send grain back, but keep one of them in Egypt. This action contrasts with their crime of selling their brother into slavery.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “bound in the house of your prison.”

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause is circumstantial-temporal.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[for] the hunger of your households.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect here has an injunctive force.

*Translator's note:* After the injunctive imperfect, this imperfect with vav indicates purpose or result.

*Translator's note:* The Niphal form of the verb has the sense of “to be faithful; to be sure; to be reliable.” Joseph will test his brothers to see if their words are true.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they did so.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a man to his neighbor.”

*Translator's note:* Or “we are guilty”; the Hebrew word can also refer to the effect of being guilty, i.e., “we are being punished for guilt.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the distress of his soul.”

*Study note:* The repetition of the Hebrew noun translated *distress* draws attention to the fact that they regard their present distress as appropriate punishment for their refusal to ignore their brother when he was in distress.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and also his blood, look, it is required.” God requires compensation, as it were, from those who shed innocent blood (see {{Genesis 9:6|Gen 9:6}}). In other words, God exacts punishment for the crime of murder.

*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause provides supplemental information that is important to the story.

*Translator's note:* “was listening.” The brothers were not aware that Joseph could understand them as they spoke the preceding words in their native language.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for [there was] an interpreter between them.” On the meaning of the word here translated “interpreter” see *HALOT* 590 s.v. מֵלִיץ and M. A. Canney, “The Hebrew *melis* (Prov IX 12; Gen XLII 2-3),” *AJSL* 40 (1923/24): 135-37.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he turned to them and spoke to them.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “took Simeon.” This was probably done at Joseph’s command, however; the grand vizier of Egypt would not have personally seized a prisoner.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he bound him.” See the note on the preceding verb “taken.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they filled.” The clause appears to be elliptical; one expects “Joseph gave orders to fill…and they filled.” See GKC 386 §120.*f*.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he did for them so.” Joseph would appear to be the subject of the singular verb. If the text is retained, the statement seems to be a summary of the preceding, more detailed statement. However, some read the verb as plural, “and they did for them so.” In this case the statement indicates that Joseph’s subordinates carried out his orders. Another alternative is to read the singular verb as passive (with unspecified subject), “and this was done for them so” (cf. NEB, NIV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the one.” The article indicates that the individual is vivid in the mind of the narrator, yet it is not important to identify him by name.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “at the lodging place.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and look, it [was] in the mouth of his sack.” By the use of the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh, “look”), the narrator invites the reader to look through the eyes of the character and thereby draws attention to the money.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and their heart went out.” Since this expression is used only here, the exact meaning is unclear. The following statement suggests that it may refer to a sudden loss of emotional strength, so “They were dismayed” adequately conveys the meaning (cf. NRSV); NIV has “Their hearts sank.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and they trembled, a man to his neighbor.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “What is this God has done to us?” The demonstrative pronoun (“this”) adds emphasis to the question.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “made us.”

*Translator's note:* The words “if we were” have been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “twelve [were] we, brothers, sons of our father [are] we.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the one is not.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “today.”
*Translator's note:* The word “grain” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* After the imperative, the cohortative with prefixed vav indicates purpose/result.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that you are not spies, that you are honest men.”

*Study note:* Joseph’s brothers soften the news considerably, making it sound like Simeon was a guest of Joseph (*Leave one of your brothers with me*) instead of being bound in prison. They do not mention the threat of death and do not at this time speak of the money in the one sack.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is not.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “is not.”

*Translator's note:* The nuance of the imperfect verbal form is desiderative here.

*Translator's note:* The nuance of the imperfect verbal form is permissive here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he”; the referent (Jacob) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Study note:* The expression *he alone is left* meant that (so far as Jacob knew) Benjamin was the only surviving child of his mother Rachel.

*Study note:* The expression *bring down my gray hair* is figurative, using a part for the whole—they would put Jacob in the grave. But the gray head signifies a long life of worry and trouble.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “to Sheol,” the dwelling place of the dead.
*Translator's note:* The disjunctive clause gives supplemental information that is important to the storyline.

*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute with the finite verb stresses the point. The primary meaning of the verb is “to witness; to testify.” It alludes to Joseph’s oath, which was tantamount to a threat or warning.

*Translator's note:* The idiom “see my face” means “have an audience with me.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “if there is you sending,” that is, “if you send.”

*Translator's note:* The verb may even have a moral connotation here, “Why did you do evil to me?”

*Translator's note:* The infinitive construct here explains how they brought trouble on Jacob.

*Translator's note:* The word “us” has been supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute with the perfect verbal form emphasizes that Joseph questioned them thoroughly.

*Study note:* The report given here concerning Joseph’s interrogation does not exactly match the previous account where they supplied the information to clear themselves (see {{Genesis 42:13|42:13}}). This section may reflect how they remembered the impact of his interrogation, whether he asked the specific questions or not. That may be twisting the truth to protect themselves, not wanting to admit that they volunteered the information. (They admitted as much in {{Genesis 42:31|42:31}}, but now they seem to be qualifying that comment.) On the other hand, when speaking to Joseph later (see {{Genesis 44:19|44:19}}), Judah claims that Joseph asked for the information about their family, making it possible that {{Genesis 42:13|42:13}} leaves out some of the details of their first encounter.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and we told to him according to these words.”

*Translator's note:* The infinitive absolute emphasizes the imperfect verbal form, which here is a historic future (that is, future from the perspective of a past time).

*Translator's note:* Once again the imperfect verbal form is used as a historic future (that is, future from the perspective of past time).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and we will rise up and we will go.” The first verb is adverbial and gives the expression the sense of “we will go immediately.”

*Translator's note:* After the preceding cohortatives, the prefixed verbal form (either imperfect or cohortative) with the prefixed conjunction here indicates purpose or result.

*Translator's note:* The pronoun before the first person verbal form draws attention to the subject and emphasizes Judah’s willingness to be personally responsible for the boy.

*Study note:* Smr reads “king” here, but the traditional reading (“angel”) may be maintained. Jacob closely associates God with an angelic protective presence. This does not mean that Jacob viewed his God as a mere angel, but it does suggest that he was aware of an angelic presence sent by God to protect him. Here he so closely associates the two that they become virtually indistinguishable. In this culture messengers typically carried the authority of the one who sent them and could even be addressed as such. Perhaps Jacob thought that the divine blessing would be mediated through this angelic messenger.

The meanings of “deliver, protect, avenge” are most fitting when God is the subject (see A. R. Johnson, “The Primary Meaning of גאל,” *Congress Volume: Copenhagen, 1953* [VTSup], 67-77).

He could be referring to the land in Shechem he bought in {{Genesis 33:18|Gen 33:18-19}}, but he mentions here that it was acquired by warfare, suggesting that the events of {{Genesis 34:25|34:25-29}} are in view (even though at the time he denounced it, {{Genesis 34:30|34:30}}). *Translator's note:* The term אַחֲרִית (akharit) refers to what is after or behind, which by extension can refer to the result, descendants, the hind part of something, or the following time (cf. *HALOT* 36). Like its Akkadian cognate, ina aḫirāt ūmī, the Hebrew phrase בְּאַחֲרִית הַיָּמִים (be’akharit hayyamim) means “in future days.” In OT literature, most predictive discourse is prophetic and consequently naming a future time period, like “days are coming” (יַמִּים בָּאִים, yammim baʾim; 20x) or “in a future time” (13x), typically occurs in prophetic speech. The description in BDB 31 s.v. אַחֲרִית overreaches the evidence to say that this is “a prophetic phrase denoting the final period of the history so far as the speaker’s perspective reaches” (cf. {{Numbers 24:14|Num 24:14}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:30|Deut 4:30}}; {{Deuteronomy 31:29|31:29}}), although several times the phrase does refer to the restoration after the Babylonian conquests. The contents of some of the sayings in this chapter stretch from the immediate circumstances to the time of the settlement in the land to the coming of Messiah. There is a great deal of literature on this chapter, including among others C. Armerding, “The Last Words of Jacob: {{Genesis 49|Genesis 49}}, ” *BSac* 112 (1955): 320-28 and B. Vawter, “The Canaanite Background of {{Genesis 49|Genesis 49}}, ” *CBQ* 17 (1955): 1-18.

It would describe Reuben as being “frothy, boiling, turbulent” as water. The LXX has “run riot,” the Vulgate has “poured out,” and *Tg. Onq*. has “you followed your own direction.” It is a reference to Reuben’s misconduct in {{Genesis 35|Gen 35}}, but the simile and the rare word invite some speculation. H. Pehlke suggests “destructive like water,” for Reuben acted with pride and presumption; see his “An Exegetical and Theological Study of {{Genesis 49:1|Genesis 49:1-28}}” (Th.D. dissertation, Dallas Theological Seminary, 1985).

*Text-critical note:* Henri Cazelles, “Shiloh, the Customary Laws and the Return of the Ancient Kings,” in *Proclamation and Presence*, eds. J. I. Durhan and J. R. Porter, 248, shows that שִׁילֹה could represent “to whom it belongs” because a scribal practice at Qumran and in Mishnaic writings was to show doubling of a consonant by preceding it with a *mater lectionis* (consonant used as vowel letter). So s-y-l-h could equal s-l-l-h, or שֶׁלֹּה, which is the way the ancient versions read it. שֶׁלֹּה can be a compound of a relative pronoun (“which”), a preposition (“to”), and archaic third masculine singular suffix (“him”). Thirty-eight Hebrew manuscripts show this variant. See Walter C. Kaiser, *The Messiah in the Old Testament,* 51, and Cazelles, 248.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew form שִׁילֹה (shiloh) is a major interpretive problem. There are at least four major options (with many variations and less likely alternatives): (1) Some prefer to leave the text as it is, reading “Shiloh” and understanding it as the place where the ark rested for a while in the time of the Judges. (2) By repointing the text others arrive at the translation “until the [or “his”] ruler comes,” a reference to a Davidic ruler or the Messiah. (3) Another possibility that does not require emendation of the consonantal text, but only repointing, is “until tribute is brought to him” (so NEB, JPS, NRSV), which has the advantage of providing good parallelism with the following line, “the nations will obey him.” (4) The interpretation followed in the present translation, “to whom it [belongs]” (so RSV, NIV, REB), is based on the ancient versions. Again, this would refer to the Davidic dynasty or, ultimately, to the Messiah.

*Translator's note:* Or “glisten from.” The adjective חַכְלִילִי (khakhlili) occurs only once in the Bible, its meaning uncertain. A possible Akkadian cognate suggests it means “dark”. The LXX interprets it as “glisten.” *DCH* also suggests “red” (*DCH* s.v. חַכְלִילִי) as a possibility. The preposition מִן (min) can indicate the source “from,” or comparison “more than.” So the possible meanings are “darker than” (NIV, ESV, NRSV), “redder than,” dark or “dull from” (NASB), “red from” (KJV) or “glisten from” (LXX). Since the context describes positive elements that Judah will enjoy as blessings, we don’t expect it to mean eyes glazed over from being drunk. Also the possible Akkadian cognate refers to darkness or gloom, not simply a dark color. Alcohol can cause capillaries to break, leading to red eyes. But whatever is going on with the eyes, the point is that Judah will have abundance to partake of. The LXX suggests a glint of happiness in the eyes spurred by drinking wine. While this may suit the context well, it is not clear that the translator wasn’t simply guessing to fit the context.

*Translator's note:* Some translate these as comparatives, “darker than wine…whiter than milk,” a reference to, presumably, a healthy appearance (so NEB, NIV, NRSV). But understood as a symbol of abundance, the dark or red eyes would be from drinking wine, and the white teeth from drinking milk.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text appears to mean “[is] a son of fruitfulness.” The second word is an active participle, feminine singular, from the verb פָּרָה (parah, “to be fruitful”). The word “son” nowhere else refers to a plant and the noun translated “branches” (*Heb* “daughters”) in the third line is a plural form whereas its verb is singular. In the other oracles of {{Genesis 49|Gen 49}} an animal is used for comparison and not a plant, leading some to translate the opening phrase בֵּן פָּרָה (ben parah, “fruitful bough”) as “wild donkey” (JPS, NAB).
